ComprehensionText:
Mr Brown had a magnificent apple tree. On this hung five ripe, red apples.

Each day, Mr Brown went out to count the apples. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5! Five ripe, red apples.

One night, a tiny, grey mouse ran up the trunk of the tree. Tip, tap! Tip, tap!

She chewed through the stem of one apple.

Plop!

It fell to the ground where the mouse family was waiting. Nibble, nibble, nibble. The mouse family soon ate up every piece of the apple then scampered back home.

The next morning, Mr Brown came out of his house and counted the apples.

1, 2, 3, 4! Only four apples!

'A tall, tall thief must have come in the night and stolen my apple,' he said. He went back into his house, very puzzled.
QuestionText: At the end of the story, Mr Brown was puzzled because
AnswerA: he thought he had not counted the apples correctly.
AnswerB: he wondered why the thief had not taken all the apples.
AnswerC: he could not find the mouse family.
AnswerD: he was not sure how the apple had been taken.

ComprehensionText:
Front Seat, No Driver
On Saturday morning, Dad and Ivy caught the first train on the city's new metro line. Ivy raced to the very front carriage. Where the driver's cabin should have been, there was only a huge window.
'Who's driving?' Ivy whispered.
'Computers,' said Dad. 'They control the speed and the stops.'
Ivy gripped the rail. The train slid into the dark tunnel, and tiny green lights flicked past like fireflies. Soon Ivy let go of the rail and pressed her nose to the glass.
At each station, glass doors on the platform opened at the same moment as the train doors. 'Those stop people falling onto the tracks,' Dad explained.
Then the train rose out of the tunnel onto a tall bridge. The city spread out below them, and Ivy spotted the roof of her own school.
At the last stop, Ivy didn't move. 'Can we go back the same way?' she asked. 'I want to sit at the front again.'
QuestionText: What was at the front of the train where the driver's cabin would usually be?
AnswerA: a huge window
AnswerB: a glass door
AnswerC: a computer screen
AnswerD: a row of seats

ComprehensionText:
The Cereal Contraption
Ruby hated waiting for breakfast, so she decided to invent a machine to make it for her.
She spent all of Saturday building. A marble would roll down a ramp of books, knock over a line of dominoes and tip a cup that tugged a string. The string would tilt the cereal box over her bowl.
'It will never work,' said her brother Max, crunching his toast.
Ruby ignored him. She tested it once, and the marble flew off the ramp. She tested it again, and the dominoes fell the wrong way. By lunchtime, the kitchen floor was a sea of cornflakes.
Ruby swept up, moved the ramp and added a wall of pencils. On the tenth try, everything worked. The marble rolled, the dominoes clicked, the cup tipped and the cereal poured perfectly into the bowl.
Max stared with his mouth open. 'Can you make one for me?'
Ruby grinned. 'Sure,' she said. 'But first, who's going to pour the milk?'
QuestionText: In Ruby's machine, what did the string do?
AnswerA: tilted the cereal box
AnswerB: knocked over the dominoes
AnswerC: rolled the marble
AnswerD: poured the milk

ComprehensionText:
Albert Namatjira: Painter of the Ranges
Albert Namatjira was born in 1902 at Hermannsburg, west of Alice Springs. He was an Arrernte man, and as a boy he came to know every hill, creek and tree of his Country.
As a young man, Albert carved and decorated wooden objects to sell. Then, in 1936, an artist named Rex Battarbee came to paint the area. Albert offered to guide him to the best places in return for painting lessons. Rex showed him how to use watercolour paints.
Albert learned quickly. He painted the red cliffs of the MacDonnell Ranges, purple hills at sunset and tall white ghost gums that seem to shine against the sky.
In 1938, Albert held his first exhibition in Melbourne. Every painting sold. People across Australia had never seen the outback painted in such glowing colours.
Albert went on to paint hundreds of pictures. Today his works hang in galleries around the country, and members of his family still paint in his style.
QuestionText: Where did Albert hold his first exhibition?
AnswerA: in Melbourne
AnswerB: in Alice Springs
AnswerC: in Hermannsburg
AnswerD: in Sydney

The Crinkly Lunchbox
On Monday, Ms Patel made an announcement. 'From now on, Tuesday will be Nude Food Day,' she said. 'That means no plastic wrappers in your lunchbox.'
Everybody giggled at the word 'nude', but Arlo groaned. His lunch was always crinkly. His sandwich came in cling wrap, his crackers in a packet and his cheese in its own plastic coat.
That night, Arlo told Grandma. She smiled and opened her cupboard. Out came a pile of cloth squares coated in beeswax. 'I made these years ago,' she said. 'Your sandwich can wear one instead.'
Grandma showed him how to warm the cloth with his hands so it folded neatly around the bread. Then they filled small containers with crackers, grapes and cheese cubes.
On Tuesday, Ms Patel held up the class rubbish bin. It was nearly empty. 'Last week, this was overflowing by lunchtime,' she said.
Arlo looked at his cloth wrap, ready to wash. 'Can we have Nude Food Day every day?' he asked.
QuestionText: The author wrote this story mainly to . . .
AnswerA: explain step by step how beeswax wraps are made
AnswerB: persuade schools to stop students bringing lunch
AnswerC: entertain while showing how to cut lunch rubbish
AnswerD: teach readers how plastic wrappers are made

Grandma showed him how to warm the cloth with his hands so it folded neatly around the bread. Then they filled small containers with crackers, grapes and cheese cubes.
On Tuesday, Ms Patel held up the class rubbish bin. It was nearly empty. 'Last week, this was overflowing by lunchtime,' she said.
Arlo looked at his cloth wrap, ready to wash. 'Can we have Nude Food Day every day?' he asked.
QuestionText: What can you conclude about why the class rubbish bin was nearly empty on Tuesday?
AnswerA: Most children had brought lunches without plastic wrappers.
AnswerB: Ms Patel had emptied the bin just before lunchtime.
AnswerC: Only Arlo had remembered that it was Nude Food Day.
AnswerD: The children had not started eating their lunches yet.

Sally Spangles was the popular young star of a TV show called Happy Families. She loved being recognised wherever she went. One day a new boy came into her class at school. Sally waited for him to ask for her autograph but he just said, 'Hi, I'm Melvin. What's your name?'

Sally was astounded. 'You mean you don't know who I am? Seriously?!' Melvin blinked at her through his large glasses. 'No, why should I?' 'Because I am the one and only Sally Spangles, star of Happy Families!' Melvin stared blankly at her. 'What's that?'

'Well, it's only one of the most popular shows on television!'

But Melvin simply shrugged his shoulders. 'Is that all? We don't have a TV at our place.'

By this time, a crowd of classmates had gathered. Surrounded by an audience, Sally instantly put on her standard act, pretending to faint. 'Quick, give me air!'

However, the rest of the class were so used to Sally's over-acting that they ignored her. They all stared at Melvin. Some gasped with disbelief, while others shook their heads with pity. A boy who didn't have a TV!!

Sally wasn't used to being ignored and she didn't like it. She glared at the newcomer but (annoyingly) Melvin stared straight back. 'Is that really so weird?' he asked mildly. 'Anyhow, I'd never have time to watch it.'

'Oh, I see! So what do you spend all your time doing then?' said Sally, her eyebrows raised.

Melvin blushed with embarrassment as he said, 'I'm guessing you don't play chess. Otherwise, you'd know that I'm the Melvin Preston: National Primary School Chess Champion!'
QuestionText: Why did Sally pretend to faint?
AnswerA: She was trying to be the centre of attention.
AnswerB: She wanted people to know she was unwell.
AnswerC: She was shocked that Melvin did not have a TV.
AnswerD: She wanted her classmates to move away from her.
